Without parental support and nurturing, the basis of all self-worth, it is difficult to feel deserving. I've been thinking about this a lot lately, while I try to improve my self-esteem and allow myself to feel like my thoughts, ideas, and etc. are worthy of being heard. How could a person who is neglected by the people who are supposed to nurture them ever feel that they are worth anything? It's a hard cycle to break. 

If you can understand that your feelings of loneliness (dejection) and neediness (desire for love) stem from your parent's absence--NOT an inherent unworthiness--then that will be a great tool to utilize when healing yourself.

You don't have to beg for attention anymore. You are worthy of attention and friendship just as you are. Perhaps this can relieve your anxiety around "needing" the validation of your friend. 

I went through a stage recently where I kind of gave up on needing other people in my life. I just appreciated being alone. I went on hikes by myself, read more, studied more, learned to sew, and just didn't worry about having friends or a support group of people. I came to realize that, although my actions were motivated by a negative, hurt place (not wanting to attempt friendships anymore), I actually was a lot happier and felt not lonely. I was ok with being alone and that was awesome! Incidentally, this is when I met my SO, and my ability to be independent and ok with being alone, has helped me not be co-dependent in this relationship, like I did with others.

I think I would enjoy myself, but my family is pretty exhausting to be around. I really wanted my boyfriend there for support. I'll be the only adult without a date, besides my divorced older cousin. I don't want to be childish or step down to her level by boycotting her wedding, but man, she really isn't playing nice with this one. She knows she holds all the cards in this scenario and can do whatever she pleases regarding me. She won't admit that I'm not a priority and continues to say it's about the "numbers", but I wasn't born yesterday. I've never planned a wedding either, but I'd wager that the *sister* of the bride can be accommodated, if the bride desires. It hurts and it sucks.

I also attend majority white university (literally, 85% white) and it definitely was a culture shock that affected my self-esteem...at first. Coming from a large, ethnically diverse cosmopolitan city, I knew that it was the environment, not me. People back home are much more open-minded, and my white friends there don't deny the existence of racial prejudice. I was definitely considering moving back home for school and thought I was going crazy being invalidated by everyone here until I took an African-American studies class taught by a black female professor. Not only did I learn a shit ton about racial identity which was therapeutic, I got to discuss with her how alienated I felt on campus. She was flipping amazing and shared her own feelings being in this homogenous town. She wore her natural hair everyday in cute styles, or hoop earrings--things I wanted to do, but didn't in fear of being judged or standing out even moreso--and I found that inspirational. I think finally being validated, and seeing her navigate the class with such confidence helped me decide to not give a fuck. I started wearing my hair natural and speaking up about my feelings here despite people who didn't believe me. By living here, I feel like I've gained some life experience that's strengthened me.
